COAL FIGHTS

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Overwhelmed by the discomfort of a life choked by black dust and random startling explosions, businesses and residents from Ogies, Mpumalanga is fighting the mines around in a human rights case

Unique Selling Point:
Louw Potgieter (80) is one of the oldest residents of Ogies -- in the last few years he started suffering chronic sinusitis or the first time in his life.

Guest house owners Annemarie and Mike Muller (late 50s) permanently carry around tissues -- but their constant health problems are the least of their worries -- what gets to them is that they may never get back the R6-million that they sunk into developing two guest houses in Ogies, after cashing in their pensions to invest in the town.

With mines booming around the town and another application pending that will take mining to within a few hundred metres of their yard, they should have made in killing in the business guest trade. In stead the town is slowly killing them.

Their home and guest houses are cracking from the constant and untimely dynamite explosions to prepare the way for mining and the heavy-duty dragline crunches away day and night, disturbing the rest of residents and visitors. A thick layer of black dust hangs in the air all the time.

Residents of the black township tell of being moved from one area to the next around town to make way for new stretches of opencast mining. Promises by the mines of proper housing result in stead in little concrete boxes without ventilation, electricity or water.

The people of Ogies have roped in human rights lawyer Zehir Omar to help them fight three mines in their area (GLENCORE, ANGLO AMERICAN and SHAFT32) on human rights grounds.

The DISRTESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES COMMITTEE that's been founded between the town and township, claims their right to a safe and clean environment is being destroyed, without them ever having been consulted on what was to come...now they sit with houses cracked and banks unwilling to touch the area, so they cannot sell up and leave.

Uniquely, two local doctors are also willing to stick their necks out to confirm that a rising incidence of respiratory diseases in the area can be attributed to the intense pollution by coal dust.

The group has had some minor success in court already this year when they managed to get a South Gauteng High Court innterdict to stop Glencore from privatising a public road for their own use...a move that would have cut off the town's access to the main school.

Omar feels that the community's problems would be completely addressed and solved if only the Department of Mineral Resources would send an inspector to the area to look at the residents complaints. Having got nowhere with getting said inspector to the area, he's approached the Public Protector (that office should really be willing and able to investigate the abuse or neglect of state institutions to enforce residents' complaints)...but the Public Protector dismissed Omar and Ogies and threaten to lump them with costs, should they pursue the matter.

For their part, all three mines deny any wrongdoing and have been fighting Omar in court.

Glencore aims to mine an area of 113m2 for another 22 years -- it denies that it's encroaching on the town...we would have to get independent expert opinion but it certainly LOOKS to the naked eye that they're closer than the 1000m buffer zone they should be.

I want to pull the focus a bit wider -- 67% of Mpumalanga is now covered by open cast coal mining -- this has cut the production of maize by a million tonnes.

According to an often-quoted study by the Northwest University on behalf of West European governments that are considering whether to re-open certain mining areas in Europe, Witbank and surroundings -- up to and including areas like Ogies, are now THE most polluted in the world of any mining area that's been the subject of study.

I want to investigate problems with breathing and water -- in Witbank (provincial capital, half hour away from Ogies) I have reports/case studies of black lung/mining tuberculosis in people who've never mined, but who live right next to mine dumps.

This is all happening in a context where the area has already paid a heavy price for virtually unrestricted coal mining -- Anglo is paying a fortune to rehabilitate the town's drinking water and there have long been sink holes and burning earth from old and abandoned coal mines.






Further information:
further background

WAKKERSTROOM (southern Mpumalanga, on border of KZN)

Last week, the coalition of eight civil society and community organisations that has been resisting the proposed coal mine inside a protected area and strategic water source area in Mpumalanga launched further proceedings in the Pretoria High Court.

These new proceedings are a judicial review application to set aside the decisions of the Ministers of Mineral Resources and Environmental Affairs to allow a coal mine to be built inside a declared protected environment, coupled with an interdict preventing the start of any activities at the proposed mining site pending the outcome of that review.

The two Ministers gave their approval for the 15 year underground coal mine proposed by Indian owned mining company Atha-Africa Ventures Pty Ltd (Atha) inside the Mabola Protected Environment outside Wakkerstroom in Mpumalanga. They did so despite a series of court challenges and appeals pending against each of the licences given for this mine, and without any public participation.

In terms of the National Environmental Management: Protected Areas Act, commercial mining is prohibited in declared protected environments unless both the Ministers of Mineral Resources and Environmental Affairs give their permission.

The coalition consists of the Mining and Environmental Justice Community Network of South Africa, Earthlife Africa Johannesburg, Birdlife South Africa, the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Federation for a Sustainable Environment, groundWork, Association for Water and Rural Development (AWARD) and the Bench Marks Foundation, and is represented by the Centre for Environmental Rights.

The Mabola Protected Environment also falls within a strategic water source area that has been identified as incredibly important and strategic to protect in the interests of all South Africans. The proposed mine area is located in that part of the Enkangala Drakensberg strategic water source area which constitutes the headwaters of the Usutu River System, via the Assegaai River. The Assegaai River flows into the Heyshope Dam, from which water is inserted into the Vaal River System via inter-basin transfer. Accordingly, the mine area is a water source of the Vaal River System, which supports Gauteng’s water needs. The Usutu River flows through Swaziland and, after joining the Pongola River, flows into Mozambique, where it is known as the Maputo River. Accordingly, the health of the Usutu River System is also relevant to South Africa’s international obligations to Swaziland and Mozambique. All of these users will all be affected if the sources of those rivers are compromised.

Atha was granted a mining right by the Minister of Mineral Resources in 2015, shortly after the declaration of the Mabola Protected Environment by the Mpumalanga MEC. Since then, Atha has received licences and approvals from the Mpumalanga environment department, the Department of Water & Sanitation, and the Department of Mineral Resources. All these approvals have been challenged by the coalition through internal appeals, and a High Court judicial review of the mining right.

The coalition believes it has good prospects of success in all these proceedings, and that the approvals will be set aside by the courts in due course. If necessary, the coalition will take this matter to the Constitutional Court.

Press Release:


Coal Wars
Desperate to maintain the value of their properties and their health, the people of Ogies on the
Mpumalanga Highveld are taking on coal mines in a massive legal battle. Carte Blanche meets residents of
the coal belt who claim government continues to issue mining licenses while their homes are being
damaged through encroaching blasting and clouds of coal dust are causing serious respiratory illnesses.



Script:


INSERT
In Springs east of Johannesburg, the law office of Zehir Omar is preparing for a David and Goliath fight as a small town tries to take on coal mining giants in Court.
ZEHIR OMAR: These are not rich people, Derek. They’re middle class to poor. I’m not asking for closure of the mines. You can’t say you fought for a country and you fought for this Constitution...and not implement it.
It started in March when Glencore (in a joint venture with African Rainbow Minerals) wanted to close a road around the Mpumalanga town of Ogies as its mine expands.
ZEHIR OMAR: I went to court urgently and I showed the court that the closure of the road was clearly illegal. And I was successful. The court granted an interdict to stop…to reopen the road. Then I went to court with an urgent application, asking the court to interdict Glencore in Ogies from causing a nuisance by the blasting activities. We expect to get a date now in September to be heard by the urgent court.
DEREK LINK: You can see how waste coal dumps have obliterated the landscape behind me – but it doesn’t stop there – mining rights have been granted for this side of the road. Work has started. This farmland is about to disappear.
Blasting gets ever closer, as do crunching excavators and thousands of coal trucks that take ore to be made suitable for sale to Eskom to generate the country’s power.
Annemarie Muller is secretary of the Distressed Mining Community of Ogies Forum.
DEREK WATTS: What is it like when there’s a big blast here?
ANNE-MARIE MULLER: It’s frightening sometimes. You can feel the vibration coming. The lights here it starts swinging, the windows it’s rattling – it’s terrible.
The forum was founded by a handful of Ogies businesspeople and residents like Phillip Maimela who fear their homes might soon be worthless if they don’t fight back.
DEREK: When did this happen, Phillip?
PHILLIP MAIMELA: January...
The Forum asked Omar to handle problems ranging from the road closure, to cracked houses, a lack of jobs for locals, to ill health. The Forum cited three big mines - only Glencore responded in any detail.
ZEHIR OMAR: I looked at the eyes of these people. What I observed is that the infliction of the denial of human rights. There’s not one, there is a host, Derek. For example, it is Section 24, protection of the environment. Section 25, property. Section 26, housing. Section 27, health care, water, social security. 28, rights of children... there’s blasting taking place, walls are cracking...this human rights abuse inflicted upon our people in Ogies, brought two otherwise disparate race groups together. Black and white are together. If I do not assist these people, who is going to assist them?
The Mullers invested their pension in a creche and guesthouse to benefit from Ogies’ mining boom. But they get no business from the mines they feel engulf them. Staff are forever cleaning up. White linen is out of the question.
ANNE-MARIE MULLER: If you touch something, it’s black. Five years ago, you heard the blasting, but you never feel it so with impact, but the past four…three, four years, it’s really getting terrible.
For Muller court action is a last resort as her complaints yielded little. Only some people’s cracked walls and windows were fixed -- but no-one is offering to buy out what she fears are fast devaluating properties.
ZEHIR OMAR: The solution could well be to buy the homes of the people, pay them a fair market value. But what the mine is doing amounts to a constructive illegal expropriation.
In a statement to us, Glencore acknowledged impacts from blasting but said several nearby mines could be responsible -- their own investigations lead them to conclude the damage is not linked to their operation.
The Mullers want to know why they’ve stopped getting reports from the seismograph they’d requested for their yard.
ANNE-MARIE MULLER: All of a sudden after the first court case of the road enclosure at the back here, then they stopped the reports. So I’ve emailed the guy and I asked him why don’t I get my reports anymore and he said to me, the mine says that he is not he is not allowed to give it to me anymore. So what do they hide?
GABRIEL DE CORT: In the house, I just spent now about R23,000 to fix all the cracks.
Vet Gabriel de Cort lives near the new expansion. With dwindling clientele, he too opened a guesthouse that’s cracking up.
The Bureau for Food and Agriculture Policy has warned that a growing, unchecked imbalance between mining and agriculture on the fertile Highveld maize belt could endanger food security.
GABRIEL DE CORT: I used to do about 64 dairies. I think I’ve got one left as they’ve all gone. And they were all in this area here, you know, where the mines are today.
Glencore says it’s committed to the progress of Ogies, and funds and manages economic development projects here and in the wider district that are well in excess of what the law requires of them.
“We take the concerns of the community seriously and make every reasonable effort to address legitimate complaints and concerns, and aim to conduct our business in an environmentally responsible manner.”
Glencore claims 1700 people would lose jobs if the Forum succeeds...ten times that many would lose a livelihood – crushing the local economy. But in Phola, across the N12, people who lined up to speak to us, say none of the mines do enough. Many relocated here to make way for mining, but after several months, in cases years, some new mine houses don’t have water or electricity.
Jan Bulunga chairs the Phola Ogies Rural Mining Forum that supports the court action, hoping it won’t stop at just one mine.
JAN BULUNGA: When they start come and mining, they come to the community and they promise community lot of things because they need the license. They say ja, on our social labour plan, we’re going to provide you with the job opportunity, business. But when they get that license from DMR...when you start to see the people that are picketing in the gate of the mine. When they blast the pollution it’s make things worse for the children. Now the children got asthma and then got sinus…
Glencore described its dust mitigation practices in detail, but added that there are many bigger culprits around.
Further east in Middelburg coal researcher and activist Tomas Mnguni works for ways to improve the toxic air that comes with coal.
THOMAS MNGUNI: This whole argument that if we get more coal plants then people will be better off, it’s not working. You find a community living a kilometre away from the power station, but they don’t have electricity. They don’t have access to water. They don’t have proper sanitation.
DEREK WATTS: It’s not for us…
THOMAS MNGUNI: It’s not for us...our people are still suffering in the process. So then you ask yourself if we produce electricity for who? And at what cost and who’s paying for that?
LINK: On windy days like these at the end of winter, a thick blanket of dust covers Ogies.
But even on good days, across the Highveld, pollution hangs around.
NorthWest University Geologist Danel van Tonder has studied the content of street dust in Emalahleni, up the road.
DANEL VAN TONDER: A lot of the material that we found that was over the limit, what we call the heavy metals, would be the stuff that actually also originate from the smelters, not just the mining. We did find the scenario a lot worse than what we anticipated, especially looking at dust pollution, because air pollution, you can divide into gasses and then particulate matter. So the particles that we found...we found what we call heavy metals that was way over the limit if you compare that to World Health Organisation standards.
For Middelburg GP Alexis Mashifane health studies of the Highveld coal impacts can’t come soon enough.
DR ALEXIS MASHIFANE: There are people who are living in other areas like Pretoria ...where’s there’s not a lot of mining, but when they come to Middelburg, suddenly they develop this respiratory illnesses, allergic rhinitis and then asthma...once they leave the area, they become well...there’s a long standing inflammatory process that happens in the small airways called bronchioles and that leads to a lot of problems, mainly the narrowing of those bronchioles and also production of mucus and they got a lot of wheezing. So some of them have hyper sensitive chests, but some do develop into asthma.
THOMAS MNGUNI: We’ve got enough information that says air pollution is directly linked to a specific set of diseases….now we could link certain pollutants to why people get heart attack...our government is paying little attention to air pollution issues and therefore our communities still struggle to understand the direct link between health and air pollution.
LINK: Scientists and activists have been warning about the rampant spread of coal mining for many years but now they say that finding a way forward without coal is no longer a green cause, but a matter of survival.
And in Ogies, it will be up to the court to decide how the Constitution must be made real.
ZEHIR OMAR: The first complaint by the people of Ogies ought to have resulted in a compliance inspector going there, camping out there for a week.
ANNE-MARIE MULLER: Why do we have to live like this? People come here and they make money out of our town. Our town is dirty...but we have to just keep our mouth shut and just go on like this. No. No, it’s wrong.
PROMOS

10
Overwhelmed by the discomfort of black dust, loud blasting and toxic air, the community of Ogies takes big coal companies to court...but do they stand a chance?


15
ANNE-MARIE MULLER: People come here and they make money out of our town. Our town is dirty...but we have to just keep our mouth shut and just go on like this. No. It’s wong.

Can the mining town of Ogies get the court to make big coal mines change their ways?


15

The town of Ogies says coal mines are harming their right to an environment that’s not harmful to health and wellbeing. But what will the court say?
ZEHIR OMAR: You can’t say you fought for this this country and you fought for this Constitution...and not implement it.

Black and white are together. If I do not assist these people, who is going to assist them? The Mullers invested their pension in a creche and guesthouse to benefit from Ogies’ mining boom. But they get no business from the mines they feel engulf them. Staff are forever cleaning up. White linen is out of the question. ANNE-MARIE MULLER: If you touch something, it’s black. Five years ago, you heard the blasting, but you never feel it so with impact, but the past four…three, four years, it’s really getting terrible. For Muller court action is a last resort as her complaints yielded little. Only some people’s cracked walls and windows were fixed -- but no-one is offering to buy out what she fears are fast devaluating properties. ZEHIR OMAR: The solution could well be to buy the homes of the people, pay them a fair market value. But what the mine is doing amounts to a constructive illegal expropriation. In a statement to us, Glencore acknowledged impacts from blasting but said several nearby mines could be responsible -- their own investigations lead them to conclude the damage is not linked to their operation. The Mullers want to know why they’ve stopped getting reports from the seismograph they’d requested for their yard. ANNE-MARIE MULLER: All of a sudden after the first court case of the road enclosure at the back here, then they stopped the reports. So I’ve emailed the guy and I asked him why don’t I get my reports anymore and he said to me, the mine says that he is not he is not allowed to give it to me anymore. So what do they hide? GABRIEL DE CORT: In the house, I just spent now about R23,000 to fix all the cracks. Vet Gabriel de Cort lives near the new expansion. With dwindling clientele, he too opened a guesthouse that’s cracking up. The Bureau for Food and Agriculture Policy has warned that a growing, unchecked imbalance between mining and agriculture on the fertile Highveld maize belt could endanger food security. GABRIEL DE CORT: I used to do about 64 dairies. I think I’ve got one left as they’ve all gone. And they were all in this area here, you know, where the mines are today. Glencore says it’s committed to the progress of Ogies, and funds and manages economic development projects here and in the wider district that are well in excess of what the law requires of them. “We take the concerns of the community seriously and make every reasonable effort to address legitimate complaints and concerns, and aim to conduct our business in an environmentally responsible manner.” Glencore claims 1700 people would lose jobs if the Forum succeeds...ten times that many would lose a livelihood – crushing the local economy. But in Phola, across the N12, people who lined up to speak to us, say none of the mines do enough. Many relocated here to make way for mining, but after several months, in cases years, some new mine houses don’t have water or electricity. Jan Bulunga chairs the Phola Ogies Rural Mining Forum that supports the court action, hoping it won’t stop at just one mine. JAN BULUNGA: When they start come and mining, they come to the community and they promise community lot of things because they need the license. They say ja, on our social labour plan, we’re going to provide you with the job opportunity, business. But when they get that license from DMR...when you start to see the people that are picketing in the gate of the mine. When they blast the pollution it’s make things worse for the children. Now the children got asthma and then got sinus… Glencore described its dust mitigation practices in detail, but added that there are many bigger culprits around. Further east in Middelburg coal researcher and activist Tomas Mnguni works for ways to improve the toxic air that comes with coal. THOMAS MNGUNI: This whole argument that if we get more coal plants then people will be better off, it’s not working. You find a community living a kilometre away from the power station, but they don’t have electricity. They don’t have access to water. They don’t have proper sanitation. DEREK WATTS: It’s not for us… THOMAS MNGUNI: It’s not for us...our people are still suffering in the process. So then you ask yourself if we produce electricity for who? And at what cost and who’s paying for that? LINK: On windy days like these at the end of winter, a thick blanket of dust covers Ogies. But even on good days, across the Highveld, pollution hangs around. NorthWest University Geologist Danel van Tonder has studied the content of street dust in Emalahleni, up the road. DANEL VAN TONDER: A lot of the material that we found that was over the limit, what we call the heavy metals, would be the stuff that actually also originate from the smelters, not just the mining. We did find the scenario a lot worse than what we anticipated, especially looking at dust pollution, because air pollution, you can divide into gasses and then particulate matter. So the particles that we found...we found what we call heavy metals that was way over the limit if you compare that to World Health Organisation standards. For Middelburg GP Alexis Mashifane health studies of the Highveld coal impacts can’t come soon enough. DR ALEXIS MASHIFANE: There are people who are living in other areas like Pretoria ...where’s there’s not a lot of mining, but when they come to Middelburg, suddenly they develop this respiratory illnesses, allergic rhinitis and then asthma...once they leave the area, they become well...there’s a long standing inflammatory process that happens in the small airways called bronchioles and that leads to a lot of problems, mainly the narrowing of those bronchioles and also production of mucus and they got a lot of wheezing. So some of them have hyper sensitive chests, but some do develop into asthma. THOMAS MNGUNI: We’ve got enough information that says air pollution is directly linked to a specific set of diseases….now we could link certain pollutants to why people get heart attack...our government is paying little attention to air pollution issues and therefore our communities still struggle to understand the direct link between health and air pollution. LINK: Scientists and activists have been warning about the rampant spread of coal mining for many years but now they say that finding a way forward without coal is no longer a green cause, but a matter of survival. And in Ogies, it will be up to the court to decide how the Constitution must be made real. ZEHIR OMAR: The first complaint by the people of Ogies ought to have resulted in a compliance inspector going there, camping out there for a week. ANNE-MARIE MULLER: Why do we have to live like this? People come here and they make money out of our town. Our town is dirty...but we have to just keep our mouth shut and just go on like this. No. No, it’s wrong. PROMOS 10 Overwhelmed by the discomfort of black dust, loud blasting and toxic air, the community of Ogies takes big coal companies to court...but do they stand a chance? 15 ANNE-MARIE MULLER: People come here and they make money out of our town. Our town is dirty...but we have to just keep our mouth shut and just go on like this. No. It’s wong. Can the mining town of Ogies get the court to make big coal mines change their ways? 15 The town of Ogies says coal mines are harming their right to an environment that’s not harmful to health and wellbeing. But what will the court say? ZEHIR OMAR: You can’t say you fought for this this country and you fought for this Constitution...and not implement it.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Overwhelmed by the discomfort of a life choked by black dust and random startling explosions, businesses and residents from Ogies, Mpumalanga is fighting the mines around in a human rights case
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Louw Potgieter (80) is one of the oldest residents of Ogies -- in the last few years he started suffering chronic sinusitis or the first time in his life. Guest house owners Annemarie and Mike Muller (late 50s) permanently carry around tissues -- but their constant health problems are the least of their worries -- what gets to them is that they may never get back the R6-million that they sunk into developing two guest houses in Ogies, after cashing in their pensions to invest in the town. With mines booming around the town and another application pending that will take mining to within a few hundred metres of their yard, they should have made in killing in the business guest trade. In stead the town is slowly killing them. Their home and guest houses are cracking from the constant and untimely dynamite explosions to prepare the way for mining and the heavy-duty dragline crunches away day and night, disturbing the rest of residents and visitors. A thick layer of black dust hangs in the air all the time. Residents of the black township tell of being moved from one area to the next around town to make way for new stretches of opencast mining. Promises by the mines of proper housing result in stead in little concrete boxes without ventilation, electricity or water. The people of Ogies have roped in human rights lawyer Zehir Omar to help them fight three mines in their area (GLENCORE, ANGLO AMERICAN and SHAFT32) on human rights grounds. The DISRTESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES COMMITTEE that's been founded between the town and township, claims their right to a safe and clean environment is being destroyed, without them ever having been consulted on what was to come...now they sit with houses cracked and banks unwilling to touch the area, so they cannot sell up and leave. Uniquely, two local doctors are also willing to stick their necks out to confirm that a rising incidence of respiratory diseases in the area can be attributed to the intense pollution by coal dust. The group has had some minor success in court already this year when they managed to get a South Gauteng High Court innterdict to stop Glencore from privatising a public road for their own use...a move that would have cut off the town's access to the main school. Omar feels that the community's problems would be completely addressed and solved if only the Department of Mineral Resources would send an inspector to the area to look at the residents complaints. Having got nowhere with getting said inspector to the area, he's approached the Public Protector (that office should really be willing and able to investigate the abuse or neglect of state institutions to enforce residents' complaints)...but the Public Protector dismissed Omar and Ogies and threaten to lump them with costs, should they pursue the matter. For their part, all three mines deny any wrongdoing and have been fighting Omar in court. Glencore aims to mine an area of 113m2 for another 22 years -- it denies that it's encroaching on the town...we would have to get independent expert opinion but it certainly LOOKS to the naked eye that they're closer than the 1000m buffer zone they should be. I want to pull the focus a bit wider -- 67% of Mpumalanga is now covered by open cast coal mining -- this has cut the production of maize by a million tonnes. According to an often-quoted study by the Northwest University on behalf of West European governments that are considering whether to re-open certain mining areas in Europe, Witbank and surroundings -- up to and including areas like Ogies, are now THE most polluted in the world of any mining area that's been the subject of study. I want to investigate problems with breathing and water -- in Witbank (provincial capital, half hour away from Ogies) I have reports/case studies of black lung/mining tuberculosis in people who've never mined, but who live right next to mine dumps. This is all happening in a context where the area has already paid a heavy price for virtually unrestricted coal mining -- Anglo is paying a fortune to rehabilitate the town's drinking water and there have long been sink holes and burning earth from old and abandoned coal mines.
metadata.Further information: further background WAKKERSTROOM (southern Mpumalanga, on border of KZN) Last week, the coalition of eight civil society and community organisations that has been resisting the proposed coal mine inside a protected area and strategic water source area in Mpumalanga launched further proceedings in the Pretoria High Court. These new proceedings are a judicial review application to set aside the decisions of the Ministers of Mineral Resources and Environmental Affairs to allow a coal mine to be built inside a declared protected environment, coupled with an interdict preventing the start of any activities at the proposed mining site pending the outcome of that review. The two Ministers gave their approval for the 15 year underground coal mine proposed by Indian owned mining company Atha-Africa Ventures Pty Ltd (Atha) inside the Mabola Protected Environment outside Wakkerstroom in Mpumalanga. They did so despite a series of court challenges and appeals pending against each of the licences given for this mine, and without any public participation. In terms of the National Environmental Management: Protected Areas Act, commercial mining is prohibited in declared protected environments unless both the Ministers of Mineral Resources and Environmental Affairs give their permission. The coalition consists of the Mining and Environmental Justice Community Network of South Africa, Earthlife Africa Johannesburg, Birdlife South Africa, the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Federation for a Sustainable Environment, groundWork, Association for Water and Rural Development (AWARD) and the Bench Marks Foundation, and is represented by the Centre for Environmental Rights. The Mabola Protected Environment also falls within a strategic water source area that has been identified as incredibly important and strategic to protect in the interests of all South Africans. The proposed mine area is located in that part of the Enkangala Drakensberg strategic water source area which constitutes the headwaters of the Usutu River System, via the Assegaai River. The Assegaai River flows into the Heyshope Dam, from which water is inserted into the Vaal River System via inter-basin transfer. Accordingly, the mine area is a water source of the Vaal River System, which supports Gauteng’s water needs. The Usutu River flows through Swaziland and, after joining the Pongola River, flows into Mozambique, where it is known as the Maputo River. Accordingly, the health of the Usutu River System is also relevant to South Africa’s international obligations to Swaziland and Mozambique. All of these users will all be affected if the sources of those rivers are compromised. Atha was granted a mining right by the Minister of Mineral Resources in 2015, shortly after the declaration of the Mabola Protected Environment by the Mpumalanga MEC. Since then, Atha has received licences and approvals from the Mpumalanga environment department, the Department of Water & Sanitation, and the Department of Mineral Resources. All these approvals have been challenged by the coalition through internal appeals, and a High Court judicial review of the mining right. The coalition believes it has good prospects of success in all these proceedings, and that the approvals will be set aside by the courts in due course. If necessary, the coalition will take this matter to the Constitutional Court.
